input: # Octal and binary are folded by the same conversion as hex, so a literal
# past the exact integer range pins them too.
# `hex:false` turns off the engine's number lexer for base-prefixed
# literals, which is what rejects `0x1F`. The uppercase `0X` form is not
# lexed as a number in any runtime: it is matched by the `uppercaseHex`
# value definition, which the option does not touch, so it keeps parsing.
# That asymmetry is canonical TypeScript behaviour, and these two rows are
# here so it is executed in all three runtimes rather than assumed.
0x1F
0X1F
# With the number lexer off, the `uppercaseHex` value definition owns the
# whole literal, so its own conversion has to round once from the exact
# integer too. Same number as the numbers.tsv rows, through the other path.
0Xa6f2f78f4f9bf44
# A byte-order mark is JSON5 whitespace (U+FEFF), so a source that is
# ONLY a BOM holds no value, exactly as a source of only spaces does,
# and resolves to the declared empty result when requireValue is off.
# An editor writes this file by itself, which is why it is a shared row
# rather than a unit case in one runtime.
// only a comment
/* only a comment */
# requireValue:false means "a source with no value resolves to the grammar's
# declared emptyResult", and that has to hold for EVERY no-value source, not
# only the exactly-empty one. TypeScript short-circuited on `` alone and let
# whitespace/comment-only sources fall out of the rules as undefined, while Go
# answered nil for all of them. These rows pin the whole set in both runtimes.
// only a comment
/* only a comment */
# Not a no-value source: a string whose CONTENTS look like a comment. The
# scan stops on the leading quote and never looks inside.
# An unterminated block comment holds no value either, but the engine's own
# unterminated_comment is the better diagnosis and must not be swallowed.
foo
# The same astral IdentifierStart seam as keys.tsv, at a VALUE position:
# with strictValue off an unquoted run is a string, and its first
# character goes through the same text check. Canonical TypeScript
# refused both of these until 2026-09-21, when the check began reading a
# code point; they were the two rows of that divergence the register
# could not hold, because it has no opts column.
𝒜
{a:𝒜}
# The control at a value position: U+1F600 is So, so it opens nothing,
# strictValue or not.
# A hash-comment-only source with requireValue ON. The guard's scan knows
# the two slash comment forms and NOT `#`, in all three runtimes, so the
# guard does not fire; the parse then fails on the comment with the
# engine's own code. Canonical TypeScript does exactly this, so this row
# pins the agreement rather than a wish. It is also the control for the
# rows below: they made the requireValue-OFF scan hash-aware and this
# answer had to stay exactly as it was.
# comment
# With requireValue OFF, a hash-comment-only source holds no value, so it
# resolves to the grammar's declared empty result exactly as the empty
# source, a run of spaces and the two slash forms already do. It did not until 2026-09-21: the scan
# did not recognise `#`, the source reached the rules, and TypeScript fell
# out with UNDEFINED where Go and Rust answered null. That was recorded in
# ../../DIVERGENCE.md as unrepairable, on the ground that teaching the scan
# the hash form would also change the control row above. It does not: the
# canonical calls the scan from separate requireValue branches, so only the
# OFF branch was told about `#`. Measured in all three runtimes before and
# after. The entry is gone and these rows replace it.
# Bite-checked by flipping the first cell below to UNDEFINED: TypeScript
# and Rust go red, Go does not, because Go returns a bare nil for both and
# its runner says so (go/parity_test.go). The null is pinned as null in the
# two runtimes that can tell the difference, and as "parsed, no value" in
# the one that cannot.
# c
# c\n# d
# c
# A bare `#` with hashComment OFF is not trivia to the scan, so the source
# still reaches the rules and is refused there. The hash-awareness is
# conditional on the option, and this row is what says so.
# c
# And a hash comment that PRECEDES a value leaves the value findable, with
# requireValue either way: the scan stops at the line terminator.
# c\n1
# A hash comment before a real value is a comment, as it should be.
# c\n1
